papers.title: Multi-source DOM inputs dictate net extra carbon mineralization in eutrophic lakes via non-linear co-metabolism effects
papers.abstract: Microbially mediated decomposition of dissolved organic matter (DOM) is a key process in the carbon cycle of inland lakes. Exogenous DOM inputs can alter the decomposition of resident lake-water DOM through co-metabolic effects (CE), yet how DOM source and addition level jointly regulate this process remains poorly understood, especially in eutrophic lakes. Here, we selected Lake Taihu, a representative hypereutrophic lake, and conducted incubation experiments by separately adding DOM derived from rainwater, leaves of aquatic plants, terrestrial litter, and treated sewage effluent to algal-rich lake water at matched carbon-addition levels. Water chemistry and DOM optical properties were used to identify factors associated with source- and concentration-dependent CE. DOM from aquatic plants and rainwater, which exhibited relatively strong aromatic and humified characteristics, induced positive CE. In contrast, terrestrial litter-derived DOM produced a weaker positive CE, while sewage-derived DOM, characterized by stronger fresh autochthonous and microbial signatures and lower average molecular weight, induced negative CE. The magnitude of CE varied nonlinearly with addition level, peaking at intermediate concentrations. CE was closely related to DOM aromaticity, humification, fresh autochthonous characteristics, and nitrogen conditions. A source-resolved scenario analysis combining estimated DOM-C inputs with source-specific CE indicated that the negative contribution of sewage-derived DOM could offset much of the positive contribution from natural sources, although the combined effect remained a potential net increase in carbon mineralization. These findings demonstrate that DOM from different environmental sources can induce CE in opposing directions in bloom-affected Lake Taihu water and that CE magnitude depends nonlinearly on loading level.

papers.title: Blood-meal analysis indicates preferential feeding on humans and non-commensal rodents by Culex mosquitoes in Tanzania
papers.abstract: Arthropod-borne viruses are important emerging and re-emerging pathogens worldwide, yet information on mosquito feeding ecology and associated transmission networks remains limited in many African regions. This study investigated mosquito host-feeding patterns and arbovirus occurrence along an urban-rural gradient in Morogoro, Tanzania. Mosquitoes were collected at four locations representing different levels of human influence during wet and dry seasons. Vertebrate blood-meal sources were identified using a Nanopore-based metabarcoding approach, while viral screening was performed using RT-qPCR assays targeting Orthoflavivirus and Alphavirus genera. A total of 8,917 mosquitoes were collected, of which more than 90% belonged to the Culex genus. Blood-meal analyses of 310 blood-fed and gravid mosquitoes identified 35 molecular operational taxonomic units, which we grouped into 11 host categories. Humans were the most frequently utilized hosts (68%), followed by non-commensal rodents (22%) and crows (18%). Culex mosquitoes showed broad host use and frequently fed on multiple taxonomic units, with an average of 1.36 taxonomic units detected per individual. Co-feeding network analyses revealed extensive host sharing between humans and wildlife, with non-commensal rodents showing significantly higher co-feeding probabilities with humans than any other host group. No human-pathogenic arboviruses were detected. Viral detections were limited to insect-specific viruses, an endogenous viral element in chromosome 2 of Aedes aegypti, and two detections of bird-infecting Bagaza virus, indicating ongoing viral circulation within the mosquito community. Our findings demonstrate broad and flexible host use by Culex mosquitoes and highlight non-commensal rodents as an underappreciated component of mosquito feeding with potential relevance for arbovirus transmission and spillover between wildlife and humans.

papers.title: A vulnerability assessment framework for terrestrial invertebrate species threatened by wildlife trade
papers.abstract: Wildlife trade is an emerging threat to terrestrial invertebrates in Australia, yet its impact on native populations remains poorly quantified. Short range endemic (SRE) species, often characterised by restricted geographic ranges, low reproductive output, low vagility, and specialised habitat conditions, are particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures, including over-exploitation via wild harvesting. Using a multi-year dataset of Australian invertebrate trade records, we identified species that are both utilised in the pet trade and exhibiting SRE traits, and assessed their risk of population decline by integrating trade frequency with species distribution, abundance, and biological vulnerability. We identified 266 species traded in Australia with an area of occupancy less than 500 square kilometres, with arachnids disproportionately represented among those at greatest relative risk of population decline from over-exploitation. While these rankings should be interpreted as a methodological demonstration rather than a definitive measure of extinction risk, they provide a transparent approach for screening species where trade pressure may intersect with biological vulnerability. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first tested approach to holistically assess this risk in invertebrates. We present a proof-of-concept framework for quantifying trade-related vulnerability in terrestrial invertebrates, providing a transferable approach that can be refined and applied across a wide range of taxa threatened by wildlife trade.

papers.title: Dog-assisted scat sampling reveals genetic diversity, structure, and relatedness in black-footed cats (Felis nigripes)
papers.abstract: Advances in molecular techniques for non-invasive genetic sampling have strengthened wildlife genetics, enabling researchers to study elusive and difficult-to-study species with minimal disturbance, and conservation detection dogs can greatly increase sample numbers and the area covered. However, this combination is rarely used in Africa and has perhaps never been applied to a small carnivore on the continent. Here we use dog-assisted scat surveys to carry out the first fine-scale population genetic study of the black-footed cat (Felis nigripes), Africa's smallest and most range-restricted endemic felid, and a threatened species for which conventional survey methods are largely ineffective. Using 130 successfully genotyped scat samples (nine microsatellite loci) from two populations about 650 km apart, we identified 65 individuals and assessed genetic diversity and fine-scale relatedness to explore aspects of dispersal and reproductive ecology. Both populations exhibited similar observed heterozygosity (Ho = 0.67-0.69) and allelic richness, with no heterozygote deficit (FIS = -0.02 to -0.08). Differentiation between the southern Namibia and central South Africa sites was low but detectable (FST = 0.03-0.05). We used pairwise relatedness and candidate pedigree results to explore hypotheses about sex-specific relatedness patterns. Female-female dyads were more related than male-male dyads at the shortest distance class (0-2 km), a pattern compatible with female philopatry. There were more half-sibling than full-sibling assignments and uneven representation of candidate fathers, which may indicate polygamy and reproductive skew. These results provide baseline genetic data for a Vulnerable species and show that this approach is feasible for Africa's small, elusive carnivores, whose dispersal, mating systems and population structure remain largely unknown. Broader spatial and temporal sampling could help assess population connectivity and reveal how threats and changing land use impact genetic diversity and structure.

papers.title: Is hidden demographic heterogeneity pervasive? Harvested birds as an example
papers.abstract: Individual demographic heterogeneity refers to the fact that individuals from a given population exposed to similar environmental conditions express different demographic traits or tactics. This heterogeneity can either be linked to factors/states such as age, sex or body condition, or be due to hidden factors/states not immediately apparent or easily characterized (hereinafter referred to as 'hidden heterogeneity'). Yet accounting for demographic heterogeneity, and more particularly heterogeneity in survival is crucial because it is an important mechanism underlying compensation processes between natural and harvest mortality. In this study, we used capture-mark-recapture-recovery data of 6 hunted species covering a large range of the demographic slow-fast continuum (61,432 individuals ringed from 1953 to 2020 among Common Teal Anas crecca, Mallard A. platyrhynchos, Common Pochard Aythya ferina, Common Snipe Gallinago gallinago, Common quail Coturnix coturnix, and Blackbird Turdus merula), to assess the presence of unexplained heterogeneity in survival with multievent models. We detected hidden survival heterogeneity in most species, even though the differences between the high and low categories of survival were often small. The probability for an individual to display a low vs high survival rate was not related to potentially important individual factors/states such as migration phenology or to morphology. The presence of hidden heterogeneity was pervasive, affecting species distributed along a relatively large spectrum of demographic strategies. This, in our opinion, supports that part of this heterogeneity in survival evidenced in our study is indeed hidden, resulting either from hidden intrinsic (inherent) individual differences of survival among individuals, or hidden extrinsic factors e.g., linked to spatial variations in hunting pressure. Our findings suggest that hidden heterogeneity needs to be explored more thoroughly in huntable species and accounted for in management policies.

papers.title: Depth structures metabolic potential and warming responses inmarine microbial eukaryotes
papers.abstract: Microbial eukaryotes are key drivers of food-web dynamics and nutrient cycling across the ocean's water column. Yet, how their metabolic potential is structured through depth remains largely unknown, limiting our ability to understand how microbial communities mediate biogeochemical transformations and how these functions may shift under climate change. Here, we combined a global-scale metagenomic analysis of tropical and subtropical samples spanning the full water column with bathypelagic metatranscriptomics to identify depth-dependent functional patterns across plankton size fractions. At depth, the functional composition of the nanoplankton size fraction was consistent with the export of surface-derived biomass, whereas the picoplankton size fraction showed signatures of resident communities, including depth-specific heterotrophic functions and bathypelagic-restricted fungal assemblages. Metabolic functional diversity was tightly coupled to taxonomic composition along the water column. Heterotrophic lineages contributed to phosphorus and sulfur acquisition at depth, revealing an undercharacterised eukaryotic role in deep-ocean nutrient cycling. Projections under end-of-century warming revealed spatially structured metabolic responses: subtropical intensification of photosynthetic capacity, subpolar stimulation of aerobic metabolism, and a decline of heterotrophic potential consistent with metabolic rebalancing within mixotrophic taxa. Our findings highlight the importance of marine microbial eukaryotes in ocean biogeochemistry, reveal their distinct functional roles across depths, and provide novel projections of how their metabolic potential may change under ocean warming.

papers.title: Effects of tree species diversity and identity on remotely sensed canopy variables in two forest biodiversity experiments
papers.abstract: Remote sensing can link biodiversity and its effects on ecosystem functioning in forests, but in observational studies environmental covariates may confound results. We tested effects of tree species richness and functional diversity on remotely-sensed canopy variables at community and species levels in two forest biodiversity experiments established under homogeneous environmental conditions. At the BIOTREE sites in Kaltenborn and Bechstedt, we combined airborne imaging spectroscopy-based vegetation indices, sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence, and land surface temperature at 1-m resolution, with ground-based tree stem growth as a productivity measure. At Kaltenborn, increasing species richness (one to four species) did not increase community productivity because of contrasting species-level responses. The normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) decreased with richness in both needle-leaved species but increased in both broadleaved species. At Bechstedt, increasing functional diversity of mixtures planted with four tree species lowered community-level normalized difference water and photochemical reflectance indices; responses differed between four functional groups of tree species. NDVI was negatively correlated with basal area; correlations among other spectral, thermal, and fluorescence traits varied among tree functional groups. These results show that forest biodiversity experiments can test remotely sensed indicators of tree diversity and ecosystem functioning and inform interpretation of observational studies.

papers.title: A leaf-carbon economy model to explain the adaptive value of low vs. high leaf mass per area as a function of habitat productivity
papers.abstract: Plant traits interact with environmental conditions to determine plant fitness. In particular, plant species with low leaf mass per area (LMA) are more common in high fertility soils and forest gaps, while plant species with high LMA are more common in low fertility soils and in shaded forest understories. It is not yet known why the adaptive value of LMA changes as a function of environmental productivity. We present a model for plant growth as a function of LMA and productivity. Our model relies on an empirically derived relationship between LMA and leaf lifespan. We are able to explain why species with lower LMA are successful in high productivity environments including environments with high availability of either light or soil nutrients, by showing that the LMA which maximizes growth rate decreases with increasing rate of carbon assimilation. We show that low LMA species are better at taking advantage of the 'high interest' environment of high productivity habitats by reinvesting assimilated carbon in new leaves and earning compound interest, while high LMA species grow more efficiently in the 'low interest' environment of low productivity habitats. This tradeoff sheds light on the adaptive value of LMA as it relates to environmental productivity.

papers.title: Fungal-bacterial interactions enhance bacterial but constrain fungal resistance and recovery to extreme heat across soil moisture levels
papers.abstract: Soil fungi and bacteria are key drivers of nutrient cycling and plant productivity in terrestrial ecosystems, yet their responses to climate extremes are rarely studied as interacting partners rather than in isolation. Moreover, it remains largely unknown how fungal-bacterial interactions regulate fungal and bacterial stability under climate extremes, particularly resistance (immediate responses to climate extremes) and recovery (responses after climate extremes cease). Here, we conducted a soil microcosm experiment with a bacterial species (Pseudomonas putida KT2440) paired with one of four Trichoderma species (T. hamatum, T. atroviride, T. koningiopsis, and T. harzianum). These fungal-bacterial pairs were then exposed to a 5-day heat event (40 {degrees}C/32 {degrees}C, day/night) followed by a 14-day recovery period (25 {degrees}C/17 {degrees}C, day/night), at two soil moisture levels (30% and 5% gravimetric water content). Our results show that fungal-bacterial interactions asymmetrically affect fungal and bacterial responses to extreme heat. Trichoderma species facilitated the resistance and recovery of P. putida density (CFUs) to extreme heat, whereas P. putida constrained the resistance and recovery of fungal biomass (ergosterol) to extreme heat, regardless of soil moisture conditions. Moreover, faster-growing Trichoderma species were associated with greater facilitation of bacterial resistance and recovery. Bacterial density also covaried positively with fungal biomass during heat stress under both soil moisture conditions, suggesting that net fungal facilitation enhances bacterial persistence under extreme heat. Together, our findings reveal that fungal-bacterial interactions can stabilize one microbial partner while increasing the vulnerability of the other, highlighting the contrasting consequences of biotic interactions under climate extremes.

papers.title: Species differentiate water uptake depths within a narrow vertical zone in temperate grasslands
papers.abstract: Whether and under which conditions coexisting species in temperate grasslands differentiate their water uptake within the shallow soil layer they share is central to understanding hydrological niche differentiation in these ecosystems. In this field study, we quantified water uptake depth of 28 coexisting herbaceous species across 74 temperate grassland plots in three regions of Germany using oxygen stable isotopes and soil water content measured at multiple depths. Species consistently differed in water uptake depth across all regions, consistent with hydrological niche differentiation. This differentiation was largely confined to the upper 30 cm of soil and became stronger as overall soil moisture declined, with plants accessing water at greater depths in drier plots. In contrast, the vertical distribution of soil moisture was unrelated to either uptake depth or species differentiation. Despite pronounced species level variation, broad herbaceous functional classifications, including grasses versus forbs and fibrous versus taprooted species, showed substantial overlap in water uptake depth. Together, our results show that hydrological niche differentiation in temperate grasslands is expressed through fine scale differences among species within a shared shallow soil domain, becomes more pronounced under drier conditions, and is poorly captured by broad herbaceous functional classifications.

papers.title: Ecological opportunity and evolutionary relatedness predict parasite sharing differently across mammalian taxonomic scales
papers.abstract: As global change brings species into new contact, understanding the ecological and evolutionary drivers of parasite sharing is essential for anticipating and mitigating disease emergence. Yet, the relative importance of geographic proximity and evolutionary relatedness among host species in predicting parasite sharing remains unresolved. We tested whether their relative importance changes across host taxonomic scale using 30,310 recorded associations between 680 mammalian and 11,107 parasite species. Geography accounted for 86.6% importance within genera, declining to 44.7% across all mammals, shifting toward evolutionary relatedness predominating. Parasite sharing increased nonlinearly with geographic proximity and host relatedness, and the overall trend varied among parasite types. Notably, accounting for host taxonomic scale improved parasite-sharing prediction accuracy. To explore the consequences of biotic homogenization, we applied a counterfactual scenario of reducing geographic distance by 99%, which increased mean predicted parasite sharing to 13.71% within genera and 1.50% at the class level. Together, these findings suggest that ecological opportunity is especially consequential among close relatives whereas evolutionary similarity is increasingly important among geographically distant species. Accounting for evolutionary scale can therefore improve sharing predictions and help identify which new host encounters warrant surveillance for cross-species transmission and disease emergence.

papers.title: Host availability, climate and pupal-stage ecology shape the predicted environmental suitability of the New World screwworm across Central and South America
papers.abstract: Background: The New World screwworm, Cochliomyia hominivorax, causes primary myiasis in warm-blooded vertebrates. Its recent resurgence in Central America has renewed the need for spatial tools that identify environmentally suitable areas and surveillance gaps. Most previous distribution models have emphasized climate and livestock, whereas ecological constraints acting during the free-living pupal stage have rarely been incorporated. Methods: We compiled 2,461 georeferenced occurrence reports from the literature across Central and South America and linked them to climate, livestock density, forest cover and superficial soil predictors. Four sequential (nested) logistic models quantified the incremental contribution of predictor blocks, compared using likelihood-ratio tests, AIC and discrimination metrics. Logistic regression and Random Forest were then compared using five-fold spatial block cross-validation, which we treat as the primary measure of generalisation, and an independent municipality-level 70:30 train-test split. Variable importance was assessed using Random Forest Mean Decrease Accuracy together with partial-dependence profiles. Because presence and pseudo-absence classes were balanced before fitting, model outputs are interpreted as relative environmental suitability rather than absolute probability of occurrence. Results: The literature database represented 2,589 infected hosts, dominated by cattle, pigs, dogs and humans. Across the sequential models, AUC increased from 0.780 for climate alone to 0.898 with livestock density, 0.908 with forest cover and 0.918 with superficial soil properties; the increment attributable to the soil block ({Delta}AUC = 0.010) was smaller than the between-fold variability observed under spatial cross-validation (SD 0.049) and is therefore reported as suggestive rather than established. Sheep and horse density and cold-quarter soil temperature showed the highest Mean Decrease Accuracy values, while silt texture ranked above cattle density and forest cover. Under spatial block cross-validation Random Forest was markedly more stable than the GLM (mean AUC 0.926 {+/-} 0.049 versus 0.814 {+/-} 0.157) and was retained as the final model. On the independent municipality-level test set it achieved AUC 0.981, TSS 0.824, sensitivity 0.850 and specificity 0.972, values we regard as optimistic relative to the spatially blocked estimates. Predicted suitability was highest across Central America and parts of northern and tropical South America. Conclusions: C. hominivorax occurrence was associated with interacting climatic, host and landscape conditions. Superficial soil variables added a small, biologically interpretable signal consistent with constraints acting during pupation, but one that lies within the uncertainty of our spatial validation and requires confirmation with independent data. The maps estimate relative environmental suitability rather than infection incidence, and are intended to identify areas where surveillance could be strengthened rather than to guide control operations directly.

papers.title: Positive relationships between interspecific association strength and elevational range overlap highlight the role of facilitation in community assembly
papers.abstract: The interplay of abiotic conditions and biotic interactions determines individual species' ranges, and by extension therefore, community assembly. To date, studies have focused predominantly on abiotic filtering (e.g., temperature) and agonistic interactions (e.g., competition) as potential drivers of community assembly; the role of facilitation in setting geographical range limits and structuring communities remains unclear. We tested how participation in compositionally distinct modules of facilitative networks of interactions in mixed-species bird flocks (MSFs) influenced interspecific elevational range overlaps across a 2000m elevational gradient in the hyperdiverse Eastern Himalaya. Species that participated in MSFs had higher average elevational range overlap compared with MSF non-participants. Positive correlations between pairwise association strength in MSFs and elevational range overlap were found for all MSF modules. We highlight the potential role of facilitation in determining species co-occurrence patterns and assembling communities across large spatial gradients.

papers.title: The ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) of Iceland
papers.abstract: The native terrestrial biota of Iceland required long oceanic journeys to colonize the island. Human colonization of Iceland, however, has allowed many less vagile species, such as ants, to reach the island. We compiled published, unpublished, and new records of ants from Iceland and evaluated the probable origin and current status of each species. We analyzed 565 records compiled by the Icelandic Institute of Natural History (1974-2020) and 84 new records (2019-2023) representing 25 species. Only five species were found living outdoors: Hypoponera ergatandria (507x indoors and 9x outdoors, mostly in geothermal areas), Lasius niger (24x indoors and 12x outdoors away from heated buildings), Hypoponera eduardi (5x only in geothermal areas), Lasius platythorax (1x near a small greenhouse and 1x in imported plant material), and Myrmica rubra (1x in an urban garden). Three ant species were exclusively found inhabiting heated buildings: Monomorium pharaonis (41x), Tapinoma melanocephalum (10x), and Monomorium nr. pharaonis (3x). Records of the remaining 17 species all appear to be based on temporary infestations, found on recently imported plant material. Previous records from Iceland of Hypoponera punctatissima appear to be based on misidentifications. Although it is possible that some ants were present before human arrival, all 25 ant species may have arrived accompanying humans. It remains to be seen whether any of these ant species are having or will have a significant impact on the native Icelandic biota. The arrival of Myrmica rubra in Iceland is particularly worrisome, given the impact this species is having in other high latitude areas it has invaded.

papers.title: Natural regeneration in tree islands drives long-term recovery of native forest-associated woody species in oil palm landscapes
papers.abstract: 1. Large-scale conversion of tropical rainforests to oil palm plantations is a major driver of biodiversity loss in Southeast Asia, particularly threatening native forest-associated plant species and their associated biota. Integrating tree islands within monocultural oil palm landscapes has emerged as a promising approach to mitigate biodiversity loss. However, their effectiveness in sustaining natural regeneration and long-term recovery of native forest-associated plant species remains unclear. 2. We analyzed temporal trajectories of diversity, abundance, and composition of naturally recruiting woody species in tree islands embedded in a monoculture-dominated landscape. We used a large-scale biodiversity enrichment experiment with 52 tree islands, varying in area (25 - 1600 m2) and planted tree diversity (0, 1, 2, 3, or 6 species), established in a conventional oil palm plantation in Sumatra, Indonesia, in 2013. 3. Across four censuses conducted between 2 and 8 years after the onset of natural regeneration, we found 82 species of recruiting woody plants (trees and shrubs) belonging to 64 genera and 34 families. At the landscape (gamma) scale, species richness and abundance increased by ~42% and ~69%, respectively, from 2018 to 2024, with shifts in community evenness and continued species arrival. After 8 years, neither richness nor abundance saturated, indicating continued accumulation of recruiting plant species. 4. Tree islands promoted natural regeneration of native diversity, with 90% of species and individuals being native. Native forest-associated species (N = 35) increased steadily at the landscape scale, while localized dominance of alien species did not indicate arrested succession. 5. At the local (alpha) scale, larger island area exerted a sustained positive effect on recruiting diversity. Higher initial planted tree diversity promoted native recruitment, particularly of forest-associated species, at earlier stages, an effect that diminished over time. 6. Synthesis and applications. Tree islands promote natural regeneration and accelerate recovery of native forest-associated diversity over extended periods, providing an effective strategy to enhance forest-associated biodiversity within oil palm landscapes. Preserving the last remaining lowland rainforests, irreplaceable reservoirs of native forest-associated species, remains essential to support continued recruitment into tree islands that can create stepping-stone habitats and a more wildlife-friendly agricultural matrix.

papers.title: Assembly of host-specific bacterial and fungal communities from soil by diverse subaerial green algae
papers.abstract: Green algae recruit microbes from their environment to the phycosphere, a region closely surrounding algal cells which is analogous to the rhizosphere of land plants. Recent work showed that subaerial green algae can recruit and assemble their phycosphere microbiota from soil-derived bacteria. However, how widespread this ability is among diverse green algae, whether host identity shapes community composition, and whether soil-borne fungi can be recruited to the phycosphere remained unclear. Here, we show that subaerial green algae spanning Chlorophyta and Streptophyta assemble distinct phycosphere communities from soil-derived bacteria and fungi, with host identity as the primary driver of phycosphere composition, both in natural soil and in a liquid mesocosm. In soil, bacterial communities were strongly reshaped by algal hosts, whereas the fungal communities responded more weakly and less consistently. In liquid system, bacterial community composition was correlated with host phylogeny. Phycosphere communities included taxa known to associate with land plants in the rhizosphere, supporting the finding that some microbial taxa associate with a wide range of photosynthetic hosts. Our findings demonstrate that the green algae capacity to assemble distinct phycosphere communities possibly predates the divergence of Chlorophyta and Streptophyta. The stronger effect of host identity on bacterial than fungal community mirrors patterns observed in land plant microbiota, suggesting that principles of host-microbe interactions are conserved across evolutionarily distant photosynthetic hosts.

papers.title: A tabular foundation model rivals established species distribution models from presence-only records
papers.abstract: Predicting where something occurs from records of where it has been observed, without reliable records of absence, is a common problem in science. Species distribution models (SDMs) such as MaxEnt address it in fields from biological conservation and climate-change assessment to the mapping of disease vectors and archaeological sites, but must be tuned for each dataset. Tabular foundation models, pre-trained on synthetic prediction tasks, predict new datasets without per-dataset training. Only one study has tested them as SDMs, and it fine-tuned on survey data from the evaluated regions. We evaluated tabular foundation models on the standard SDM benchmark (225 species in six regions, with independent presence-absence surveys), under the protocol used to compare 21 methods, and on 120 virtual species with known distributions. Without tuning, a tabular foundation model, TabPFN 3.5, equalled the best published approach, a five-model ensemble (mean AUC 0.732). Fine-tuned on presence-background tasks from other regions, it became the best single model on the benchmark (0.736), outperformed MaxEnt (0.728) and boosted regression trees after correction for multiple comparisons, and was better calibrated than MaxEnt, although six regions were too few to establish the advantage for new regions. Fine-tuning on presence-absence surveys of other species helped only when they came from the evaluated regions. On virtual species, it recovered simple additive relationships less well than regression-based methods but complex ones at least as well when records were unbiased, and was worse with environmentally biased records. Tabular foundation models are competitive SDMs without per-dataset tuning, but they are sensitive to environmentally biased records.

papers.title: Population dynamics in extreme environments: shared histories of strong selection lead to predictable patterns across separate high-elevation populations of small mammals
papers.abstract: Many frameworks exist to identify species that are vulnerable to environmental change, but we still generally lack the ability to anticipate species' responses when changes occur. Exploring patterns of trait evolution along environmental gradients could help this process: conditions become more predictable and less variable at the ends of gradients, with past studies hypothesizing that consistently harsh environments will result in predictable evolutionary patterns. To test this hypothesis, we characterized genetic and phenotypic variation, as well as selection on this variation, in deer mice (Peromyscus maniculatus) along two transects spanning from 2120-4200m in the Colorado Rocky Mountains, U.S.A. We found that both genetic and phenotypic variation declined with elevation, that high elevation populations had higher rates of survival, and that fewer traits influenced survival at high elevations. These results suggest extreme environments may lead to predictable consequences for populations and provide a basis for forecasting population vulnerability to environmental change.

papers.title: Slowed aquatic invasion coincides with intensified research and prevention in Minnesota, USA
papers.abstract: Prevention is often the most cost-effective expenditure of limited environmental management resources. While demonstrating that harms occur without prevention is relatively straightforward, showing harms have lessened due to prevention--proving its effectiveness--is not, in part because it requires counterfactual data (i.e., quantification of harms that did not occur and then attributing these to prevention). Here, we attempt to measure aquatic invasive species (AIS) prevention effectiveness in Minnesota, USA, where AIS, their management, and research have increased since the 1980s. We showed the rate of new aquatic invasions slowed alongside intensified prevention investment starting around 2015. Further, mechanistic simulations grounded in real boater movement and boat inspection effectiveness data suggested prevention may have reduced new invasions of two high-priority AIS by 20-53% over a ten-year span. We argue our evidence strongly supports long-term statewide prevention, monitoring, and research.

papers.title: Phenotypic variation in divergent mitochondrial haplotypes in migratory three-spined stickleback
papers.abstract: Mitochondria are essential components in life-sustaining organismal processes. The mitochondrial genome can be influenced by selection, and divergent mitochondrial haplotypes have substantial potential to affect interspecies variation in life-history and physiology, yet little is known about whole organism phenotypic changes that might accompany mitochondrial genomic divergence. Three-spined stickleback on the Scottish island of North Uist provide a model to study this as their populations exhibit a well-mixed nuclear genome, yet two highly diverged mitochondrial haplotypes ( trans-Atlantic and European). Three-spined stickleback were sampled from six lochs to investigate associations between mitochondrial haplotype and phenotypic traits including organ size, body size, and ovule volume/clutch size, as well as citrate synthase enzyme activity. Results showed that mitochondrial haplotype has an influence on male gonadosomatic index (GSI) and potentially citrate synthase (CS) enzyme activity. Differences in male GSI may be explained by the timing of male spermatogenesis or potentially a need for larger testes in European haplotype fish. While no other phenotypic trait showed differences between mitochondrial haplotypes, there were many differences between sexes and populations e.g. in body size and organ/muscle size.

papers.title: Disease dynamics during ecosystem restoration and faunal reassembly
papers.abstract: Biodiversity recovery is increasingly promoted as a strategy for restoring ecosystem services, including the regulation of infectious diseases. However, it remains unclear how the potential for pathogen transmission interacts with the timing of biodiversity recovery and the life history of the recovering species to shape the disease dynamics during restoration. Here, we developed a stochastic multi-host metacommunity epidemic model to investigate how the timing of the establishment of slow life history species, pathogen transmissibility, and host-community succession jointly influence disease outcomes in recovering ecosystems. Pathogen transmissibility (R_0) was the dominant predictor of epidemic intensity, whereas the delayed timing of establishment of slow life history species during restoration emerged as a major ecological determinant of pathogen persistence. Delayed establishment of slow life-history hosts consistently increased disease prevalence and persistence by prolonging the dominance of highly competent fast life-history hosts. Generalized additive models revealed a strong interaction between delayed timing of slow life-history species establishment and pathogen transmissibility, explaining more than 90% of the variation in pathogen persistence. The influence of timing of establishment of slow life history species was weak for pathogens with low transmission potential but increased markedly as R_0 increased. Sensitivity analyses further showed that, once pathogen transmissibility was controlled, timing of establishment became the strongest predictor of persistence, whereas among-host spillover transmission primarily influenced the speed of epidemic spread. In contrast, maximum species richness had comparatively little influence on disease outcomes, indicating that the functional composition and assembly timing of recovering communities may be more important than richness alone for predicting disease dynamics. Together, these results demonstrate that disease regulation during ecosystem restoration depends not only on pathogen transmissibility, but also on the life history traits and the timing of establishment of species within recovering communities. Our findings identify life history traits and the timing of when functional communities are restored as a key ecological lever influencing long-term pathogen maintenance in restored ecosystems.

papers.title: Two decades of EU pesticide substitution have not reduced impacts on stream invertebrates
papers.abstract: Chemical regulation assumes that withdrawing hazardous substances and replacing them with alternatives reduces environmental harm. We tested this premise within the EU pesticide regulatory framework using a 23-year record of event-driven pesticide exposure and stream-invertebrate communities from 152 German agricultural streams sampled between 1998 and 2021. Neither pesticide toxic pressure nor pesticide-related invertebrate impairment showed a detectable decline over time, and an improvement equivalent to one ecological status class can be excluded. Dominant toxicity drivers shifted from organophosphates to neonicotinoids and subsequently to pyrethroids, yet the relationship between toxic pressure and community effects remained consistent despite their distinct modes of action. Sustained toxic pressure reflected three mechanisms: successive chemical substitution, prolonged approval periods, and continued exposure to substances no longer authorised as plant protection products. Substitution thus changed which chemicals harm streams, not how much. Measured field outcomes must become the benchmark of pesticide regulation.

papers.title: Gregariousness can promote invasion success of pest insects while higher environmental heterogeneity decreases it
papers.abstract: Climate change and environmental homogenization are expected to facilitate the expansion of many forest pest insect species and increase the vulnerability of forest ecosystems to insect outbreaks. At present, we lack empirical data on how the antipredator defence traits of pest insects interact with the local environmental conditions and shape outbreak risk. Here we study this and ask 1) how the antipredator defence strategy of pest insects shapes survival under naturally varying predator community, and 2) how is predation risk shaped by the diversity and structure of forests? We tested these questions by conducting a field predation experiment with artificial prey system (prey items made from edible dough) where we manipulated the gregariousness, unpalatability and defensive colouration of prey and tested their effects on prey survival. Additionally, we measured environmental variables and invertebrate predator community structure along the prey transects to analyse how they shape overall predation risk. Our results show that the predation risk was always lowest for gregarious prey irrespective of other defence strategies. Furthermore, our results indicate that predation pressure was lower in more homogenously structured forest areas or areas with a weak quality deadwood continuum in comparison to locations with more natural state forests and good quality deadwood continuum. Altogether, our results suggest that gregariousness can facilitate pest insects to form outbreaks by increasing their survival against generalist predators. However, by maintaining higher heterogeneity in forests, it is possible to ensure higher predation pressure to regulate their population growth.

papers.title: Tree cavities as attractors: an experimental test of the effects of woodpecker legacy on local bird activity and species richness
papers.abstract: Tree cavities, whether excavated by birds or formed through wood decay, are key structural features of forest ecosystems. They are critical resources for secondary cavity users and influence breeding bird assemblages by affecting the occurrence and abundance of certain species. However, the effect of an individual cavity on fine-scale bird activity, independently of the surrounding habitat context, remains poorly understood. Here, we experimentally tested the effect of cavity presence on bird activity in a coniferous forest in southern Poland. We installed pairs of standardized, debarked snags, each consisting of one snag with an artificial entrance resembling a woodpecker-excavated cavity and one control snag without a cavity entrance. Bird presence and activity were monitored using camera traps and vegetation structure was quantified around each snag. The presence of a cavity entrance had a positive effect on visitation rates and species richness. Snags with cavity entrances received 114% more bird visits than control snags (4.5 [95% CI: 3.1-6.5] vs 2.1 [1.4-3.2]) and were visited by 48% more species (2.0 [1.5-2.6] vs 1.3 [0.9-1.9]). In addition, greater canopy closure around snags was associated with higher visitation rates and species richness. Our study demonstrates that a single cavity can act as a fine-scale attractor for forest birds. These findings highlight the role of cavities and cavity-bearing trees in shaping spatially heterogeneous patterns of fine-scale habitat use by birds.

papers.title: Energetic and functional development of soil food webs along secondary succession
papers.abstract: 1. As ecosystems develop, aboveground biomass and belowground organic matter accumulate, while energy turnover declines. This trend is largely supported by vegetation studies, but remains unexplored for soil food webs that channel the majority of energy in terrestrial ecosystems. 2. Here, we tested whether successional theory applies to soil food webs across size-based compartments, ranging from microfauna (nematodes) to macrofauna (soil arthropods and earthworms), along a secondary succession in southwestern China, using an energy-flux approach. To assess whether forest restoration by planting follows natural succession, we also compared spruce and larch plantations with secondary birch forest of the same successional stage. 3. Supporting expectations of reduced energy turnover, the results showed an increasing animal biomass-to-energy flux ratio and a functional shift from herbivory-dominated (green) to detritivory-dominated (brown) energy channelling along succession. Soil food web compartments showed contrasting trends: macro-food webs shifted towards bacterial energy channels with decreasing predation, while micro-food webs maintained similar bacterial/fungal energy flux ratios and tended towards increasing predation. The larch plantation supported lower animal biomass than the secondary birch forest, whereas the spruce plantation did not differ. We further found that energy flux correlated positively with microbial biomass and soil animal diversity, but negatively with litter biomass during succession. 4. Overall, we expand successional theory by revealing the transformations in energy use and pathways within soil food webs along secondary succession, thereby advancing understanding of ecosystem functioning and guiding ecosystem restoration. Our results further suggest that tree plantations do not necessarily replicate the belowground development of natural succession, which should be considered in ecosystem restoration.

papers.title: Examining urban weed response to elevated salt levels
papers.abstract: Stressors from the urban environment cause adverse effects on city-dwelling organisms. While there is evidence that some species are adapting to urban stressors, such as the urban heat island and impervious surfaces, other stressors such as road salt are less studied. We investigated whether plants are adapting to elevated salt concentrations with two common garden experiments using three common weed species: Veronica arvensis, Stellaria media, and Lamium purpureum. We collected plants from parks around Baltimore, MD, USA, collecting plant maternal lineages from roadside soils (i.e. higher soil salinity) and inner park soils (i.e. lower soil salinity). We hypothesized that roadside lineages would tolerate salt treatment better than park lineages. In our germination experiment on wild-collected seeds, we observed a non-significant trend where the germination rate of roadside L. purpureum lineages was reduced less by salt treatment than for park genetic lineages, while S. media had similar declines between groups. In our greenhouse experiment on the F1 generation, roadside V. arvensis lineages displayed a less adverse reaction to salt treatment than park V. arvensis lineages. L. purpureum did not display this difference, but roadside lineages of both species exhibited less tissue damage overall. The results of our experiments were likely influenced by the maternal environment, and work on F2 generations is required to confirm them. Our findings show some support for urban salt tolerance adaptation, and point to the heterogeneity of the urban environment and the complexity of plant reactions to salinity.

papers.title: Invasion analysis for structured populations: analytical principles and numerical workflows
papers.abstract: All real populations show some form of structure--differences among individuals, such as life stage or physiological condition, that shape a species' ability to persist. Yet it remains challenging to incorporate population structure into models of species interactions. We provide a general framework for studying competition in structured populations by quantifying species' invasion growth rates. The crux of our approach is separation of timescales: the initial dynamics of a structured population depend on how exactly it is introduced, but these transient differences do not affect long-term invasion success. Depending on the research question, the relevant long-term growth rate when rare may equivalently be derived using analytical separation of timescales, matrix population theory, or numerical simulations. Using case studies spanning developmental stage, environmental state, and infection status, we illustrate how our methodology derives simple, ecologically meaningful invasion conditions for a variety of systems. Finally, we extend the approach to fluctuating resident dynamics, showing how to use simulations or a general mathematical framework known as Floquet theory to correctly quantify invasion growth. By unifying the quantitative methods of population biology and community ecology, our framework will allow ecologists to study species persistence and coexistence across a greater variety of demographically complex systems.

papers.title: Primary vitamin B12 limitation and widespread stress in Antarctic phytoplankton
papers.abstract: Iron is considered the dominant limiting or colimiting nutrient for phytoplankton growth in the Southern Ocean. However, strong competition and limited biosynthesis capabilities for vitamin B12 (cobalamin) within the microbial community creates conditions suitable for cobalamin limitation. Through a nutrient enrichment experiment in the Amundsen Sea, we show that growth in a phytoplankton community comprising diatoms and prasinophytes was limited primarily by cobalamin and secondarily by iron. Protein biomarkers across a broad area of the Southern Ocean further indicate widespread cobalamin stress within diatoms and Phaeocystis. As warming-induced melting of ice-shelves increases iron supplies in the coastal Southern Ocean, shifts from iron to cobalamin limitation favor mixotrophic flagellates with low cobalamin requirements, altering community composition and function.

papers.title: Interspecific social contacts spread gut microbiota in wild rodent communities
papers.abstract: Background: The mammalian gut microbiota influences a wide array of host phenotypes and varies substantially among individuals. Among conspecifics, microbiota composition is strongly shaped by microbial transmission through social interactions, yet the extent to which such transmission also occurs across species boundaries remains poorly understood. Here, we combine high-resolution tracking data collected over more than 10 months with gut microbiota profiling to examine social associations, space use, and microbiota similarity among individuals of three sympatric rodent species - wood mice (Apodemus sylvaticus), yellow-necked mice (A. flavicollis) and bank voles (Myodes glareolus), in two woodlands. By integrating multi-species social networks and spatial overlap with individual microbiota data, we test how both conspecific and interspecific interactions shape gut microbiota composition. Results: At both study sites, social associations strongly predicted microbiota similarity among conspecific individuals, whereas spatial proximity consistently predicted microbiota similarity among interspecific pairs. In addition, social associations between mice of different species predicted microbiota similarity, although this effect was weaker than that observed within species and was asymmetric, with evidence for stronger microbial transmission from wood mice to yellow-necked mice than vice versa. By focusing on species-indicative bacterial taxa, we further show that wood mice with more social connections to yellow-necked mice harboured a greater richness of gut bacteria typical of yellow-necked mice. Conclusions: Together, these results demonstrate that individual-level social behaviour can influence gut microbial transmission across species boundaries, particularly among closely related species with overlapping ecological niches. Interspecific social interactions may therefore represent an underappreciated pathway for the acquisition of novel gut symbionts in multi-species communities.

papers.title: Microscale nonrandomness revisited: An overlooked predictor of ecological change
papers.abstract: Abrupt ecological transitions have driven the development of early warning signal metrics that track how ecological systems respond as external conditions gradually change and systems approach transitions between states. However, their generality and applicability remain uncertain, particularly for short-term ecological dynamics that can occur without directional external change. To address this gap, we propose a general framework based on the hypothesis that microscale nonrandomness, quantified from frequency distributions or spatial patterns, predicts subsequent short-term rates of change in populations and interactions, as well as current macroscale ecosystem states. We applied the framework to four datasets: time series from an incubation experiment of phytoplankton-parasitic chytrid interactions; spatiotemporal field observations of leaf beetles on willow trees and aphids in a crop system; and spatial snapshot data linking soil surface characteristics with aboveground and soil ecosystem properties in a forest vegetations-soil system. We quantified microscale nonrandomness using Morisita I_{delta} from frequency distributions and Moran's I and SADIE from spatial patterns. Across all systems, models incorporating microscale nonrandomness metrics consistently showed greater cross-validated predictive performance than those based on macroscale variables or spatial averages alone. Although their relative performance varied among systems, frequency-based metrics performed as well as or better than spatially explicit metrics in some cases. The consistent improvement across contrasting systems supports the broad applicability of this framework, including under limited data conditions. This framework broadens ecological forecasting to short-term, continuous dynamics beyond those associated with directional environmental change.
